title: Legal computability: Rules never exhaust legal outcomes
desc: Contrasts formal determinacy with realist prediction and empirical jurimetrics, without rejecting coherent doctrine or limited computability.

kps.k: The cluster frames legal computability as a dispute over whether rules determine outcomes, rather than simply whether machines can process legal texts.
kps.d: The introductory chapter to Is Law Computable? contrasts axiomatic law with realist accounts of contextual, politically influenced adjudication. Langdell's Legacy describes Langdell's belief that lawyers could discover a small set of absolute principles in cases and deduce outcomes from them. The introductory chapter distinguishes this case-based approach from Leibniz's reliance on domestic and natural law. These accounts establish a historical ambition for legal prediction, not evidence that deduction reliably predicts judgments.

qs.q: Langdell believed that law could be simplified into a "comparatively few absolute rules." 1 44 Once "found," these rules could be categorized into doctrinal frameworks from which lawyers and judges could deduce the outcomes of cases.
qs.a: Langdell's Legacy: Living with the Case Method · Academia · 1991

qs.q: Whereas Leibniz considered a combination of existing domestic and natural law as their source, Langdell believed legal ax- ioms—or to use his term: ‘principles’—were empirically derived as they were in the natural sci- ences.
qs.a: Is Law Computable? From Rule of Law to Legal Singularity (introductory chapter to Is Law Computable? Critical Perspectives on Law and Artificial Intelligence) · Academia · 2020

kps.k: Realist critiques separate predicting what courts will do from deriving what rules supposedly require.
kps.d: Jurimetrics presents Holmes's predictive conception alongside the realist claim that competing rules can justify contrary outcomes and that opinions may rationalise decisions rather than explain their formation. Its author goes further, asserting that genuine issues are resolved at a largely subconscious level; the excerpts offer argument and cited scholarship, not measured evidence for that assertion. The sources also resist a single anti-formalist position: Jurimetrics distinguishes Pound's principle-oriented Sociological Jurisprudence from realist emphasis on particular cases, while acknowledging their shared concern with social adaptation and indistinct boundaries.

qs.q: In every actual case, they point out, there are rules that can be applied which lead to contrary results.

kps.k: Rejecting complete determinacy does not require abandoning regular rules or coherent doctrine.
kps.d: The Is Law Computable? chapter presents Dewey as valuing definite rules while treating attainable certainty as contingent on social facts: established customs support predictability, whereas innovation and changing relationships weaken it. The Force of Law gives formalisation a complementary institutional role. Judges adapt rules to concrete disputes; scholars integrate those changes into coherent doctrine that helps constrain arbitrary judgment. This contrasts with accounts that treat doctrinal reasoning chiefly as retrospective justification, without restoring the claim that rules mechanically settle every case.

qs.q: For Dewey, no legal argument could be validly represented as a deductive inference, and law never accurately represented with deductive axiomatic systems, arguing:        There is of course every reason why rules of law should be as regular and as definite as pos-       sible.
qs.a: Is Law Computable? From Rule of Law to Legal Singularity (introductory chapter to Is Law Computable? Critical Perspectives on Law and Artificial Intelligence) · Academia · 2020

qs.q: Through the more or less extensive freedom of interpretation granted to them in the application of rules, judges introduce the changes and innovations which are indispensable for the survival of the system.
qs.a: The Force of Law: Toward a Sociology of the Juridical Field · Academia · 1987

kps.k: Jurimetrics calls for empirical investigation rather than replacing one speculative jurisprudence with another.
kps.d: The author criticises both traditional philosophy and newer psychological or symbolic explanations for retaining speculative methods beneath changed vocabulary. Observation and investigation, rather than introspection, form the proposed next step. This is a methodological programme, not an empirical demonstration. For the computability debate, it implies that claims about what determines judgments require investigation; neither formalist confidence nor realist scepticism alone establishes a system's predictive capabilities.

qs.q: This is simply a new jurisprudence with a new vocabulary The argument seeks to substitute a modem analysis for an ancient one, but the tradi- tional techniques are still in use.
qs.a: Jurimetrics — The Next Step Forward · Academia · 1949

qs.q: If mankind is capable of learning anything, it should have learned by this time that it can solve no problems by introspection, but only by investigation.
qs.a: Jurimetrics — The Next Step Forward · Academia · 1949

kps.k: Predictability and cost-benefit calculation capture only part of the legal function described here.
kps.d: Can Robots Be Lawyers? cites Cooter's instrumental account of compliance alongside Waldron's emphasis on procedure and argument and Ewing and Kysar's account of participation and reason-giving. These attributed positions broaden the question from forecasting sanctions to preserving opportunities to make claims, contest accusations and advance reasons. The practical implication is that predictive success would not, by itself, establish equivalence to legal practice. The fragment does not establish the article author's conclusion about computers practising law, and the cluster supplies no AI performance findings.

qs.q: Economic models of law typically accept the ‘bad man’ approach and add a rationality element to it: a rational ‘bad man’ decides whether or not to obey the law by calculating his own benefits and costs, including the risk of punishment.”).
qs.a: Can Robots Be Lawyers? Computers, Lawyers, and the Practice of Law · Academia · 2017

kps.k: Legal systematisation also reflects institutions and information tools, not only theories about law.
kps.d: Langdell's Legacy reports Gilmore's qualified suggestion that the National Reporter System helped drive black-letter systematisation, supplementing the account centred on Langdell's intellectual influence. The Force of Law likewise describes practitioners using digests, form books and legal databases to meet urgent, case-specific demands. Together, these accounts place legal knowledge tools within professional practices rather than treating their existence as proof that law forms a closed deductive system. The publishing argument remains a historical interpretation; the supplied passage does not explain the reported difficulties caused by the reporting system.

qs.q: Grant Gilmore suggests that this systematization was brought about not only by Langdell's attitudes but by the establishment of the National Re- porter System.
qs.a: Langdell's Legacy: Living with the Case Method · Academia · 1991

qs.q: Rather than resorting to theoretical treatises of pure law, they employ a set of professional tools developed in response to the requirements and the urgency of practice -- form books, digests, dictionaries, and now legal databases.
qs.a: The Force of Law: Toward a Sociology of the Juridical Field · Academia · 1987

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources collectively accept the proposition that legal rules do not mechanically or exhaustively determine outcomes, and they materially develop it in several directions. Their common reasons are that adjudication involves context, policy, social change and interpretive choice; competing rules may support contrary results; and prediction captures only part of law’s procedural and reason-giving function. They nevertheless preserve an important role for regular rules and coherent doctrine: judicial interpretation adapts law to concrete disputes, while scholarly formalisation stabilises doctrine and constrains overt arbitrariness. Other extensions locate systematisation partly in publishing and professional information tools and insist that claims about adjudication or computability require observation rather than jurisprudential speculation. Material internal variation concerns emphasis rather than overall direction: realist accounts stress indeterminacy and retrospective rationalisation; Dewey combines anti-deductivism with a commitment to definite rules; the sociology of the juridical field gives doctrine a constructive institutional role; jurimetrics redirects attention toward empirical investigation; and the fragment on robots foregrounds participation and reason-giving but provides limited evidence of its author’s overall conclusion. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of academia and research generally, and their number does not indicate prevalence.

qs.q: In every actual case, they point out, there are rules that can be applied which lead to contrary results.
qs.a: Jurimetrics — The Next Step Forward · Academia · 1949

qs.q: Legal scholars, through the work of rationalization and formalization to which they expose the body of rules, carry out the function of assimilation necessary to ensure the coherence and the permanence of a systematic set of principles and rules.
qs.a: The Force of Law: Toward a Sociology of the Juridical Field · Academia · 1987

elens.an: The curated pre-2015 sources collectively accept the principal proposition that legal rules do not exhaust or mechanically determine outcomes, and they materially develop it in three ways. First, Langdell's Legacy historicises complete deductive determinacy as Langdell’s attributed ambition rather than a demonstrated feature of law, while adding that publishing infrastructure helped produce black-letter systematisation. Second, Jurimetrics supplies the strongest anti-determinist argument: competing rules may support contrary outcomes, and formal reasoning may rationalise rather than generate decisions; it also insists that these claims require observation and investigation rather than speculation. Third, The Force of Law preserves a substantial role for doctrine: judicial interpretation adapts rules to concrete disputes, while scholarly formalisation maintains coherence and constrains overt arbitrariness. The material internal variation is therefore not over whether rules mechanically settle every case, but over how strongly to distrust doctrinal reasoning and what constructive role systematisation retains. Jurimetrics is comparatively sceptical about rules and syllogistic explanation, whereas The Force of Law treats interpretive flexibility and coherent doctrine as complementary institutional functions. Langdell's Legacy contributes a historical and infrastructural explanation rather than an independent theory of adjudication. These sources are a curated set and should not be treated as representative of all foundational scholarship.

qs.q: In every actual case, they point out, there are rules that can be applied which lead to contrary results.
qs.a: Jurimetrics — The Next Step Forward · Academia · 1949

qs.q: Legal scholars, through the work of rationalization and formalization to which they expose the body of rules, carry out the function of assimilation necessary to ensure the coherence and the permanence of a systematic set of principles and rules.

elens.an: The selected 2015–2022 sources support the proposition that legal outcomes and legal practice cannot be exhausted by determinate rules or prediction. The introductory chapter provides the clearest support: it contrasts Langdell’s axiomatic ambition with realist objections that adjudication is shaped by experience, politics, consequences and changing social conditions. Its treatment of Dewey also preserves the proposition’s qualification that rejecting complete deduction does not mean rejecting regular, definite rules or limited predictability. The fragment from Can Robots Be Lawyers? supports the same overall direction more indirectly by presenting procedure, argument, participation and reason-giving as legal values beyond settled rules and sanction prediction. There is material variation in emphasis and evidential strength: the first source directly develops a jurisprudential dispute over determinacy, while the second reports attributed scholarly accounts and does not reveal enough of the author’s surrounding argument to establish a full position on machine legal practice. Neither source supplies empirical findings about AI performance or demonstrates how much legal work is computable, so their support is conceptual and historical rather than experimental.

qs.q: Holmes’ enduring contribution to jurisprudence was rejecting the deterministic and nonpolit- ical conceptions of law advanced by legal formalists like Langdell who regarded law a consistent set of rules and norms from which a ‘right’ answer could always be derived.
